title: There Will Be Blood. "I drink your milkshake" scene -- was there deeper significance in this statement?

commenti.body:
Near as I can tell it's just Daniel's chosen metaphor to condescendingly explain to Ely not only that Ely lost, but how he was able to outmaneuver him.


It just happened to become an iconic line because the delivery of it as a summary of their lifelong competition was so engrossing.


I don't recall milkshakes making an appearance prior to this. I believe when HW and Daniel go out to lunch and Daniel berates the other table of men, HW does *not* have a milkshake ordered but that would be the scene for it and it lacks Ely in the scene for the callback to work.

Milkshakes are treats you give to children. By using a Milkshake metaphor Daniel is calling Eli a child. He is dumb, naive, and in over his head. Daniel is basically telling Eli that he lost before he even walked through the door.

It's the story of America, isn't it? A bunch of Europeans come over and establish a nation in the backs of people they perceived as lesser than them, ruthlessly and methodically, and ultimately succeed, leaving their descendants to reckon with their actions. Daniel Plainview is exactly that.
I thought I'd read something to that effect. It was like, a political statement of some sort.

It's a real quote. From imdb trivia:


*The infamous "I drink your milk-shake!" is, in part, a real quote. Paul Thomas Anderson found the metaphor in congressive transcripts from the 1920s Teapot Dome scandal, in which Secretary of the Interior Albert Fall was convicted of accepting bribes for oil drilling rights to various lands. According to Anderson, "I think it was Albert Fall, who was asked to describe drainage before Congress. And his way of describing it was, 'If you have a milkshake and I have a milkshake, and my straw reaches across the room ...' I'm sure I embellished it and changed it around and made it more Plainview. But Fall used the word milkshake, and I thought it was so great. It was mad to see that word among all this official testimony and terminology - a fucking milkshake. I get so happy every time I hear that word."*

My interpretation of that infamous line is that Daniel is referring to has been that Daniel will take anything, even a small luxury such as a cold dessert, from Eli. The fact that he precedes it with "...if you have a milkshake, and I have a milkshake, and I  have a straw..." also suggesting that he has more tools and more power to continue to (literally) siphon anything good that Eli might have, or enjoy.   


I also can't totally verify this but Paul Thomas Anderson said that he lifted the line almost verbatim from an actual oil tycoon, which is particularly rich. https://cultrface.co.uk/the-origin-of-the-milkshake-line-in-there-will-be-blood/

I’m not sure if this information has been verified, but I remember reading that the “milkshake” line was lifted from actual remarks (i.e., audio recordings unearthed during PTA’s research process) made by a Republican Senator who was accepting illicit payments from oil companies in exchange for access to federal land. At the same time—who cares? “Death of the Author” or bust. We determine whether or not it has deeper significance, and I really dig your very valid interpretation.
I agree about the childhood connotation. But to me it was more about Daniel being childish, like he has finally released to completely infantile bullying.

I thinknno I think it's an example of what he did.  I think sometimes we all get hung up in deeper meaning.  It could have been a glass of water or a can of beer it would have ment the same.  I drink your milkshake seems more poetic

The way I read it is: 

He's patronising and belittling and hatefully sneering towards Eli with this childish metaphor delivered in a mocking way as though to a literal child. 

It's him ramping up his unhinged excitement and his dehumanisation of Eli before the violence that follows. The physical violence is merely part of the ongoing escalation of disrespect, of how much he hates Eli for being weak and naive and everything he cannot stand (and has done his best to do away with) in himself.

Within that scene specifically it refers to the Bandy Tract already having been purchased (it's more of an easement) by Plainview, and he is flaunting this to Eli as he comes to inform him that Bandy is dead and they can drill the land for oil. I think it alludes to the hyper-competitive nature of capital and the feeling of malevolent vindication that comes with rising above ones rivals. Also, Plainview went into Little Boston and feigned benevolence and good will, hiding his unbridled desire for success and wealth under this masquerade. A complete gentrification and almost usurpation of the place. He takes advantage of it and uses it to benefit himself, and did not, as he claimed in his big mendacious speech about bread, have any noble intentions there.  And perhaps this is a stretch, but I think it may also refer to Daniel's manipulation of the church for his own ends. Bandy did not accept Plainview's purchase until he was baptised, and so in this way Plainview was utilising Eli's church and religion for his own economic means, 'drinking from his milkshake'. Really a fantastic line. An encapsulation of the whole movie and Daniel's character, not to mention hilarious, and delivered with perfection. One of my favourite scenes in any film.
